name: Dolcetto

lines.s10: Dolcetto is the soft, dark red Piedmont drinks young: black plum and blackberry with a dry, bitter almond finish.
lines.s20: Dolcetto is the early ripening red of Piedmont, grown around Dogliani and Alba on the cooler slopes Nebbiolo will not take. It is dark and dry, with black plum, blackberry and a bitter almond finish, soft in acidity and drunk young.
lines.s45: Dolcetto ripens early and drinks early. It is a red of Piedmont, at home around Dogliani and Alba on the cooler slopes that Nebbiolo will not take. In the glass it is deep purple, with black plum and blackberry. It is soft in acidity, with a little grip and a dry, bitter almond finish. Most is kept in steel and bottled young, so the fruit stays in front. Pour it slightly cool with salumi, agnolotti or a mushroom pizza. Little sweet one is what Dolcetto means, though the wine is dry: the name is thought to describe the grapes, low in acid and sweet off the vine.
lines.sale: Dolcetto is dark, soft and ready now, a red that asks for no patience and no decanter. With the agnolotti or a mushroom dish, a glass of Dogliani served a touch cool is my choice.

glass.lead: Black plum and blackberry in a deep purple glass, soft in acidity, with a little grip and a bitter almond finish.

ladder.where: The higher, cooler Langhe slopes and Dogliani
The lower hills around Alba, Diano d'Alba and Acqui

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low to medium, tannin medium with a slightly bitter edge, alcohol medium, body medium; deep purple ruby in colour.

home.home: Piedmont, on the higher and cooler slopes of the Langhe, where it ripens weeks before Nebbiolo. Dogliani and Diano d'Alba are its DOCGs and Dolcetto d'Alba the everyday bottle. It is usually kept fresh in steel and drunk within a few years.
home.abroad: Liguria calls it Ormeasco, around Pornassio, where it makes a firm red and a rosé called Sciac-trà. Beyond Italy it is rare: a little in Australia and the United States.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; a touch cooler for a young bottle.
service.glass: A standard red wine glass; a young Dolcetto needs no great bowl.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary: it is made to be poured young and fresh.
service.age: Within two or three years; Dogliani from good sites keeps a few more.

gentle acidity and dark fruit beside salt and fat
bitter almond and black plum sit well with mushrooms
soft tannin and dark fruit meet fat and char

guest.q: Dolcetto means little sweet one. Is it a sweet wine?
guest.a: No, it is dry. The name is thought to describe the grapes, which are low in acid and taste sweet off the vine.

guest.q: How is it different from the Barbera?
guest.a: Both are dark, everyday reds of Piedmont. Barbera is sharp and juicy with little tannin; Dolcetto is softer in acidity, with a little more grip and a bitter almond finish.

guest.q: Do I need to let it breathe?
guest.a: No. It is made to be poured young and fresh, and a few minutes in the glass is all it needs.

compare.tell: Barbera is as dark but sharply acidic, with less tannin; Dolcetto is softer in acidity and rounder, with a dry, bitter almond finish.
Gamay is paler and tarter, with raspberry and sometimes banana; Dolcetto is darker, softer in acidity and firmer, with black plum and bitter almond.
Nebbiolo is pale garnet with high acidity and fierce tannin; Dolcetto is deep purple, low in acidity, soft and ready young.

profile.st: Deep purple ruby · Body medium · Acid low to medium · Tannin medium, with a bitter edge · Alcohol medium · Dry
profile.fruit: Black plum, blackberry, black cherry; riper black plum from the lower, warmer hills
profile.other: Bitter almond on the finish, liquorice and anise; little or no oak, since most is kept in steel and drunk young
profile.tell: Deep colour, soft acidity and a dry, bitter almond finish: dark like Barbera, but rounder and lower in acid
profile.regions: Piedmont: Dogliani, Diano d'Alba, Dolcetto d'Alba and Acqui; Liguria as Ormeasco di Pornassio
profile.confuse: Barbera is as dark but sharply acidic with less tannin; Gamay is paler and tarter; Nebbiolo is pale and far firmer

cards.front: Dolcetto: what does the name mean, and is the wine sweet?
cards.back: Little sweet one. The wine is dry; the name is thought to describe the grapes, low in acid and sweet off the vine.

cards.front: Dolcetto: its two DOCGs in the Langhe, and its Ligurian name?
cards.back: Dogliani and Diano d'Alba. In Liguria, around Pornassio, it is Ormeasco, with a rosé called Sciac-trà.

cards.front: Dolcetto blind: which structure and finish set it apart from Barbera?
cards.back: Deep colour like Barbera, but low to medium acidity, a little more tannin and a dry, bitter almond finish.

questions.q: A red poured blind is deep purple and soft, with black plum and blackberry, low acidity, some grip and a bitter almond finish. Which Piedmont grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour with low acidity and a bitter almond finish is Dolcetto. Barbera, the nearest wrong option, is as dark but sharply acidic, with less tannin; Nebbiolo is pale and fiercely tannic.

questions.q: A guest translates Dolcetto on the list as little sweet one and asks for something dry instead. What do you tell her?
opts: It is dry; the name describes the grapes
It is sweet, made from dried grapes
It is off dry, with a little sugar left
It is a sweet sparkling red from Acqui
questions.exp: Dolcetto is a dry red; the name is thought to describe grapes low in acid and sweet off the vine. The sweet sparkling red of Acqui, the nearest miss, is Brachetto.

questions.q: On a Ligurian wine list a guest finds Ormeasco di Pornassio and asks which grape is in the bottle. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Ormeasco is Liguria's name for Dolcetto, grown in the hills of Pornassio as a firm red and a rosé called Sciac-trà. Rossese, the nearest miss, is a different Ligurian red.

sources.title: Ente Turismo Langhe Monferrato Roero: the Dolcetto grape

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. A thin grape: the profile is written new and agrees with the Régionale row (cool to moderate, acidity low, body and tannin medium, black plum, blackberry, liquorice and almond, low acid, the name little sweet one, soft and dry, drunk early).

Piedmont facts (early ripening on the higher, cooler slopes Nebbiolo refuses, Dogliani and Diano d'Alba the DOCGs, Dolcetto d'Alba the everyday bottle, kept fresh in steel, Dogliani aged a few years) and Ormeasco with the rosé Sciac-trà around Pornassio stand on the Codex's Piedmont and Liguria records. Dogliani a DOCG since 2005 and Dolcetto alone stands on two Langhe sources.
The name thought to describe grapes low in acid and sweet off the vine stands on a grape reference and a trade glossary; the Codex states only the meaning, little sweet one.

The ladder's cool and moderate rungs are an honest inference from the Codex's cool to moderate climate and the Piedmont record's sites (Dolcetto on the higher or cooler slopes), not a sourced tasting contrast; a checker may prefer a single region named on each rung.

The named notes anise and almond skin are a taster's naming beside the Codex's liquorice and almond; a checker should weigh them. Violet, often given in trade notes, is left out for want of a firm source.

Left out: the Victorian vines planted in the 1860s and long sold as another grape, said to be among the oldest Dolcetto anywhere; the sources are a producer's own pages and trade writing under a living name.
The Codex's Piedmont trap calls Dolcetto's tannin moderate and its Régionale row gives tannin 2 of 3; one trade source calls the grape quite tannic and another soft. The entry keeps medium.
